definitions.explanation: Indicates two actions happening simultaneously. The main action is in the second clause.
Expresses a concessive contrast, similar to のに but more formal. Often used in written language.

examples.japanese: {音楽|おんがく}を{聞|き}きながら{勉強|べんきょう}する。
examples.english: I study while listening to music.

examples.japanese: {歩|ある}きながら{話|はな}しましょう。
{朝|あさ}ごはんを{食|た}べながら{新聞|しんぶん}を{読|よ}むのが{毎日|まいにち}の{習慣|しゅうかん}です。
examples.english: Reading the newspaper while eating breakfast is my daily habit.

examples.japanese: {知|し}っていながら{教|おし}えてくれなかった。
examples.english: Although they knew, they didn't tell me.

examples.japanese: {残念|ざんねん}ながら、その{日|ひ}は{参加|さんか}できません。
examples.english: Unfortunately, I cannot attend on that day.

notes:
ながら has two main uses: simultaneous actions and concessive contrast.

SIMULTANEOUS ACTIONS (sense 1):
- Attach to the verb stem (ます-form without ます)
- The subject of both clauses must be the same person
- The main action is the second clause; ながら marks the secondary action
- Example: {食|た}べながら{話|はな}す (talk while eating — talking is the main action)

CONCESSIVE USE (sense 2):
- More formal and literary than のに or けど
- Common set phrases: {残念|ざんねん}ながら (unfortunately), {少|すく}ないながら (though few)

WATCH OUT:
- ながら requires the same subject in both clauses. Use {間|あいだ}に when the subjects differ.
